chapter: Family lore, Boston and Europe with Sam Price
title: Benny Morton's growl versus J. J. Johnson's technique
summary: He calls Morton's growl part of his tone but J. J. just a technician where everything goes by.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Oh, that's it, they did work together. I saw the picture of them too in the book and I was wondering if that was - ... You were also telling us yesterday a little bit of how you reacted to trombone players such as Jay Jay Johnson, Benny Green, and their style. You said that their style was a little too technical to suit you?
No, I didn't say they - I said Jay Jay.
Just Jay Jay. But did that apply at all to - because around that time a lot of the younger trombone players were using more and more...

I haven't heard anybody with the style of Benny Morton, because most of the time when he plays, he growls, but not like Tricky Sam growled. That was part of his tone; that's the way he played. But Jay Jay Johnson, that was nothing but just technician, everything is going-going-going-going, and you don't know what's happening. I didn't; maybe they did.
Did you know a trombone player by the name of Jimmy Cleveland?
Jay Jay was one of the trombonists that changed the style of trombone playing.
